answer:
A fever is your body turning up its own thermostat on purpose to help fight an infection. When germs like bacteria or viruses get in, immune cells release signalling molecules called pyrogens, mainly interleukin-1, TNF-α and IL-6. These reach the hypothalamus, the part of the brain that controls body temperature, and trigger it to make prostaglandin E2, which raises the temperature the body aims for [1]. Your body then works to reach that higher target. Blood vessels in the skin narrow to hold in heat and you shiver to make more, which is why you feel cold and get chills as a fever starts. When the infection clears, or a drug like ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin production, the target drops back down and you sweat and flush to cool off [1].

The benefit is that heat seems to help the immune system work better. It slows the growth of some bacteria, makes neutrophils (a type of white blood cell) better at killing them, and helps activate T cells [1]. Animals have used raised body temperature against infection for hundreds of millions of years. Scientists still aren't sure how much the mild heat harms germs directly, as opposed to simply helping immune cells and chemicals move where they're needed [2]. A fever isn't always helpful, though. If the immune system releases too much of these signals, as in severe sepsis, it can be dangerous or even fatal [1].
